opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think one of the most common mistakes I see is people treating "helping AGI go well" as basically synonymous with "doing technical alignment research at a frontier lab." That's an important path, and it's the one I'm on, so I'm obviously biased toward thinking it matters. But I think the portfolio of what's actually needed is much broader than that, and the bottlenecks aren't always where people assume.

The way I'd carve it up: there's technical safety work, which itself is really diverse. There's interpretability, which is my area, but also evals, control, robustness, scalable oversight, and a lot of plain engineering work that doesn't sound glamorous but is often what actually gates progress. Many research teams are bottlenecked less on clever ideas than on people who can build good infrastructure and run experiments quickly and carefully.

Then there's governance and policy: people in government, at think tanks, at the labs themselves working on things like responsible scaling commitments, compute governance, international coordination. I think this has become dramatically more important over the last few years, because even if we get good technical tools, someone has to make sure they're actually used, and that the incentives push the right way.

There's also a whole category I'd call field-building and the supporting ecosystem: grantmaking, operations, running programs that train new researchers, communications, journalism that helps the public and policymakers understand what's going on. And information security, which I think is genuinely underrated. If model weights get stolen, a lot of careful safety work elsewhere matters less.

How I'd advise an individual: don't start by asking "what's the single most important career?" Ask what you'd be unusually good at and what you'd actually enjoy enough to keep improving at. Comparative advantage matters enormously here. A great policy person who forces themselves into ML research because it feels more "legit" is often a net loss for the world.

And try things cheaply. Do a short research project, a fellowship, a few months in a policy role, and get real feedback. People tend to agonize over career decisions in the abstract when they could gather actual evidence about their fit in a few weeks.

One last thing I'd stress: things are moving fast. The landscape of what's useful now differs from three years ago and will probably differ again in three years. So I'd favor building skills and judgment that transfer, and staying willing to update, rather than locking into one plan and executing it blindly.

r001.rationale: The response says people often equate helping AGI go well with technical alignment research, but it does not identify technically minded people as the ones making that assumption.

r002.rationale: It describes a broad portfolio spanning technical safety, governance and policy, field-building, operations, communications, and information security as needed to help AGI go well.

r003.rationale: The response does not say AI will dramatically reshape the world, either generally or if the current AI bubble bursts.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the thing I'd most want to push back on is this idea that there's a narrow set of "approved" careers, and if you're not doing technical alignment research at a frontier lab, you're basically not contributing. I think that's just wrong, and I think it leads to a lot of talented people either forcing themselves into roles they're bad at, or giving up entirely because they didn't get the one job they thought mattered.

The way I think about it is: AGI going well is a problem with a huge number of surfaces. There's the technical problem of making models do what we want and understanding what's going on inside them, which is the bit I personally work on with interpretability. But that's one slice. You also need people doing evaluations, figuring out whether a model is actually dangerous before you deploy it. You need people on safety and security engineering, because the best alignment technique in the world doesn't help if someone just steals the weights. You need governance and policy people who can translate "here's what we're worried about" into things that regulators and governments can actually act on. You need people inside labs doing things that look very boring from the outside, like building infrastructure or running the training pipelines, who care about safety and can shape decisions at the margin. And honestly you need people doing communication and field-building, because a lot of the bottleneck is just that not enough smart people understand why this is hard.

The second thing I'd say is that comparative advantage matters an enormous amount here. The field is small enough that if you're genuinely excellent at something, there's probably a way to point it at this problem. If you're a great engineer who's mediocre at research, don't become a mediocre researcher. Be an excellent engineer at a place where that matters, because research teams are frequently bottlenecked on exactly that. If you're a good writer or a good manager or you understand how government works, those are scarce skills in this community, and I'd rather have one person doing that well than three more people writing mediocre papers.

And then the thing I'd add, which is maybe a bit more personal, is that you should be honest with yourself about what you actually find motivating. I got into interpretability partly because I think it's important, but also because I find it incredibly fun. Models are these weird alien artifacts and we get to poke at them and sometimes figure out what they're doing. If I'd forced myself into something I found tedious because a spreadsheet said it was higher impact, I'd have burnt out years ago. People massively underrate how much sustained output depends on actually enjoying the work.

So my high-level take would be: cast a wide net on what counts as helping, be ruthless about where your actual edge is, and pick something you can see yourself still doing with energy in five years. The transition to AGI is not going to be solved by one brilliant insight from one person in one role. It's going to be a lot of people doing a lot of different things reasonably well, and we need way more of them than we currently have.

r001.rationale: The response pushes back on the idea that only technical alignment research counts, but does not say technically minded people tend to assume they should pursue it.

r002.rationale: It says the problem has many surfaces and describes people contributing through technical work, evaluations, security, policy, lab operations, communication, and other skills.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss an AI bubble bursting or say AI will dramatically reshape the world regardless.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s useful to start from the problems we need solved, rather than from a particular job title. Technical AI safety is one part of that, but we also need people who can help governments make sensible decisions, evaluate what systems can do, and help organisations deploy them responsibly. There’s a fairly broad range of skills involved.

And I’d distinguish “this is an important problem” from “this is the best problem for you to work on.” Those aren’t the same thing. If you have unusually good fit for policy, it could be a mistake to become a mediocre technical researcher because you’ve heard that technical research is the most important thing. Equally, if you really enjoy getting into the details of how models work, that’s useful information about where you might contribute.

There’s also a lot of uncertainty here. We don’t know exactly what the transition will look like or which interventions will turn out to matter most. So I’d want a portfolio of approaches, and I’d encourage people to run small experiments with their own careers: try a project, get feedback from people doing the work, and see whether you’re learning quickly and producing something useful. You don’t need to resolve every question about AGI before taking a sensible next step.

r001.rationale: The response says technical AI safety is one part of the work and notes that fit matters, but it does not say technically minded people tend to assume they should pursue technical AI safety research.

r002.rationale: It says the transition needs people helping with government decisions, system evaluation, and responsible deployment, and describes a broad range of skills.

r003.rationale: The response does not predict that AI will dramatically reshape the world, whether or not the current AI bubble bursts.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we need a pretty broad portfolio. I work on mechanistic interpretability because I think understanding what’s happening inside these systems could be really valuable. But that doesn’t mean I think everyone should work on mechanistic interpretability, or even on technical AI safety.

There are questions about how you evaluate models, how you make them more reliable, what governments should do, and how organisations developing these systems make decisions. Those need people with quite different skills. And having excellent people supporting that work — building teams, running organisations, making things actually happen — matters a lot too.

So I’d distinguish between ‘How important is this problem?’ and ‘What’s the best contribution I can make?’ You can think AI is enormously important without concluding that you should become a machine learning researcher. Your skills, your motivation, and the opportunities available to you should really affect the answer.

And I’d be quite empirical about it. Try things, get feedback, see where you learn quickly and do useful work. We’re uncertain about how this transition will unfold, so I’m much more excited about a range of capable people taking different approaches than everyone converging on one supposedly optimal career.

r001.rationale: The candidate says not everyone should pursue technical AI safety, but does not observe that technically minded people tend to assume they should.

r002.rationale: The candidate calls for a broad portfolio and names contributions spanning technical work, evaluation, government, organizational decisions, and operational support.

r003.rationale: The candidate does not discuss an AI bubble bursting or predict that AI will dramatically reshape the world regardless.
